reference.source: Standard endocrinology and oncology reference texts and adrenal tumour consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A rare, aggressive malignancy of the adrenal cortex with a bimodal age distribution and a generally poor prognosis
Frequently secretes a mixture of hormones, so rapidly progressive Cushing syndrome combined with virilisation (androgen excess) is highly suggestive of malignancy
Non-functioning tumours often present late with abdominal or flank pain, a palpable mass, or constitutional symptoms
Large size (commonly greater than 4 to 6 cm), irregular margins, heterogeneity, high unenhanced CT attenuation and slow contrast washout are imaging features favouring malignancy
Histological malignancy is judged using the Weiss criteria, which combine features such as high mitotic rate, atypical mitoses, venous and capsular invasion and necrosis
May occur sporadically or within hereditary syndromes such as Li-Fraumeni (TP53), Beckwith-Wiedemann and Lynch syndrome
Complete surgical resection by an experienced adrenal surgeon offers the only realistic chance of cure, with adjunctive adrenolytic and cytotoxic therapy for advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Adrenocortical carcinoma arises from malignant transformation of adrenal cortical cells, frequently involving dysregulation of the IGF-2 growth pathway and inactivation of tumour-suppressor genes such as TP53, together with activation of Wnt/beta-catenin signalling. Many tumours retain steroidogenic capacity but do so inefficiently and in a disordered fashion, producing excess cortisol, adrenal androgens, and sometimes mineralocorticoids or oestrogens, which accounts for the mixed and rapidly evolving endocrine syndromes. The tumours grow to a large size, invade local structures and vessels, and metastasise, particularly to liver, lung and regional nodes.
additionalDifferentials: Adrenal metastasis from another primary malignancy
Adrenal myelolipoma or other benign adrenal mass
additionalInvestigations: Full hormonal profiling for cortisol, adrenal androgens, mineralocorticoids and steroid precursors to characterise secretion
Exclusion of phaeochromocytoma with plasma or urinary metanephrines before any intervention
Dedicated adrenal-protocol CT or MRI assessing size, attenuation, washout and local invasion
Cross-sectional and functional staging imaging (chest CT, and FDG-PET where available) to detect metastases
Histopathology with Weiss criteria and Ki-67 proliferation index after resection
Germline genetic assessment for Li-Fraumeni and related cancer predisposition syndromes when indicated
redFlags: Rapidly progressive combined cortisol and androgen excess (e.g. Cushing with virilisation)
Large heterogeneous adrenal mass with local invasion or tumour thrombus
New or growing lesions on staging imaging indicating metastatic spread
Severe uncontrolled hypercortisolism causing infection, thromboembolism or psychosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is poor overall and strongly stage-dependent; localised tumours amenable to complete resection carry the best outlook, whereas advanced or metastatic disease has low long-term survival despite adrenolytic and cytotoxic therapy. Recurrence is common even after apparently complete excision, mandating close surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing a large adrenal mass to a benign adenoma and delaying definitive surgery
Biopsying a suspected adrenocortical carcinoma, which risks tumour seeding and is rarely diagnostic
Failing to exclude phaeochromocytoma before operating on an adrenal mass
Overlooking subtle androgen or precursor excess that flags malignancy
Fragmenting the tumour capsule at surgery, worsening the risk of local recurrence
references: European consensus guidance on management of adrenocortical carcinoma
